title: Risk-Based Prioritisation
summary: Risk based prioritisation means ordering remediation work by the realistic harm a weakness can cause in this specific environment, rather than by severity score or by the order a scanner printed its output. It combines the technical severity of a flaw with exploitability, whether the affected component is actually reachable and exposed, the value of the asset, and the controls already in place. In a working vulnerability management programme it drives the weekly queue that engineers actually pull work from, and it justifies why a medium finding on an internet facing payment service can outrank a critical finding on an isolated test host. The common mistake is to treat the scanner severity as the decision itself, which collapses a judgement about context into a single number and produces both neglected real risks and wasted effort on findings that nothing can reach.

beginner.definition: Risk based prioritisation means deciding which security problems to fix first by thinking about real harm. It looks at how serious a weakness is and how easy it is to use. It also checks how important the affected system is to the business. Two identical weaknesses on two different systems may not deserve the same urgency.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most teams cannot fix every finding at once. A long list with no order means urgent problems wait behind harmless ones. Attackers use the weaknesses that are easy to reach and valuable to them. If you fix by score alone, you may spend weeks on a system nobody can touch. Good prioritisation puts your limited time where the real danger is.
howItWorks: Collect findings from scanners, penetration tests, and reports from the teams who run the systems.
Check each finding against the real environment, asking whether the component is exposed and reachable.
Add context such as data sensitivity, business criticality, and any control that already blocks the weakness.
Combine severity and context into a risk level, then publish the ordered list to the teams.
Set response times for each level, and track whether the work is really finished.
Review the model after incidents, because real events show which signals were misleading.
beginner.example: Imagine a building with two broken window locks. One is on the ground floor beside a busy street. The other is on the fourth floor and the window does not open. Both locks are equally broken, but only one lets a stranger inside. A good caretaker fixes the ground floor lock today and notes the other for later. Risk based prioritisation is that caretaker's reasoning written down as a rule.
takeaways: A severity score describes a flaw, not the risk in your environment.
Exposure and business value change how fast a finding must be fixed.
Publish one ordered queue so engineers know what to work on next.

objectives: Explain why scanner severity alone is a poor basis for a remediation queue.
Describe the context factors that turn a technical finding into a business risk.
Explain how response targets are set for each level of risk.
Identify the trade offs between fixing quickly and fixing the most dangerous issue.
Outline how a prioritisation model is validated after real incidents.
